ECE 6390 / Antennas and arrays

Aperture addition

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how the aperture field distribution determines an angular radiation pattern.

Each illuminated aperture point contributes a field with a direction-dependent path phase. In this scalar one-dimensional model, F(θ) is proportional to ∫Eₐ(x) exp(jkx sin θ) dx.

Uniform illumination over width a produces a sinc-shaped field factor, with first null at sin θ = λ/a. Increasing electrical width makes contributions cancel at a smaller departure from boresight.

An edge amplitude taper can reduce sidelobes while broadening the main beam. Separately normalizing each curve hides absolute gain differences. In a discrete equal-amplitude exercise, amplitude tapering changes a constraint; phase choices and allowed element locations are separate design variables.

Example

For a uniform width a = 4λ, the first null is at asin(1/4) ≈ 14.5°. This is a field zero and therefore also a power zero.

    Practice

    1. Why can a tapered pattern look better in sidelobes without establishing a larger absolute peak gain?

    Ask which information is removed when every pattern is divided by its own peak.

    Peak normalization preserves shape ratios but removes the peak scale. Absolute gain needs the complete intensity integral, radiated-power normalization, and applicable efficiency factors.
